## Now

I'm finishing an M.S. in Psychology: Data Science in Human Behavior at UW–Madison (expected December 2026). My capstone, **Digital-Mailroom**, is with American Family Insurance and asks a practical question: how do you cut the cost of AI inference while reading documents better, not worse? My part is the engineering: a pipeline that routes each document to the cheapest step that can handle it, and the scoring that shows whether the routing works.

## Featured Projects

::: {.cards}
::: {.card cover="digital-mailroom"}
### [Digital-Mailroom](projects/digital-mailroom.qmd)
[Capstone · American Family Insurance]{.kicker}

Five Python packages and one LangGraph pipeline that route legal documents to the cheapest step that can handle them. Prompt experiments are judged by fixed rules against known labels, not by another model, and the whole run repeats in Docker.
:::

::: {.card cover="mailroom-ml"}
### [Mailroom-ML](projects/mailroom-ml.qmd)
[Training, evaluation & calibration]{.kicker}

A ModernBERT classifier that calibrates its own confidence, answers the easy documents itself and passes the rest to an LLM. It serves on CPU through ONNX, with a Modal fallback, and a leak audit caught a label leak in my own training data.
:::

::: {.card cover="neuron-atlas"}
### [Neuron Atlas](projects/neuron-atlas.qmd)
[Mechanistic interpretability · live browser model]{.kicker}

Explore and steer all 8,192 neurons of TinyStories-8M in the browser, with random-direction controls and replayable findings. Larger Qwen studies are recorded offline.
:::

::: {.card cover="wave-laboratory"}
### [Wave Laboratory](projects/wave-laboratory.qmd)
[Side project · simulation & graphics]{.kicker}

A real-time 3D ocean in the browser, built on spectral wave physics. Set a sea state and watch a container ship pitch and roll through it, with wave gauges and seakeeping statistics alongside.
:::
:::

## What I'm interested in

I came to machine learning through psychology, and it shapes what I work on. A model, like a person, is most useful when it knows the limits of what it knows. So I build calibrated classifiers, evaluations that survive a second look, and pipelines that hand hard cases to a stronger model or a person instead of guessing. Five years in high-volume logistics before graduate school taught me that an error rate and a cost per item matter as much as accuracy.

Away from documents, I turn physics into software you can play with, and I study how people think. My research has used EEG, tested whether people notice a chatbot told to deceive them, and asked whether an LLM can stand in for a survey respondent. So far it cannot beat simple baselines.
